# Judges 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — Israel’s Sin and Forty Years of Philistine Oppression

The seventh recorded apostasy in the book of Judges. “Again the Israelites did evil” resumes the familiar cycle: sin → bondage → repentance → deliverance → rest → sin again. The “evil” is understood as idolatry, specifically serving the gods of the Philistines (cf. 10:6). (Gill, https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/13.htm; Precept Austin, https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_13_commentary)

The Philistines were non-Semitic “Sea Peoples” who settled the coastal plain. They were not Canaanites but foreign conquerors. Their pentapolis comprised Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-13.html)

The forty-year oppression is the longest in Judges and notable because, unlike previous cycles, **there is no record of Israel crying out to God**. This silence suggests hardened hearts — spiritual apathy deeper than before. Samson would only begin deliverance; complete deliverance would wait for Samuel and David. (Precept Austin, https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_13_commentary)

G. Campbell Morgan called Samson’s story “the story of a great opportunity and a disastrous failure in the case of a man who might have wrought a great deliverance but failed.” (Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-13/)

## v. 2 — Manoah and His Barren Wife

Manoah (“rest”) was from Zorah, about 14 miles west of Jerusalem in the territory of Dan. His wife is unnamed in the text; the Talmud (Baba Bathra 91) calls her Hazelelponi or Zelelponi (“the shadow falls on me”), referencing 1 Chronicles 4:3. (Ellicott; Gill, both cited above)

Her barrenness places her in a line of barren women who bore significant children: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and later Elizabeth. The double expression “barren and had no children” is a pleonasm characteristic of ancient narrative style, emphasizing the human impossibility of the situation. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)

## v. 3 — The Angel of the LORD Appears

The Angel of the LORD (Hebrew *mal’ak YHWH*) appears to the woman — not to Manoah. Ellicott notes that Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom suggested this was Phinehas, but “nothing can be clearer than that … a supernatural being is meant.” Ellicott compares it to Judges 6:11, Genesis 18:10, and Luke 1:11–28. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-13.html)

**Key theological debate — the identity of the Angel:** Many conservative Protestant commentators identify this figure as a **pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany)**. David Guzik writes, “this was Jesus on a special mission, appearing as a man before His incarnation in Bethlehem.” Gill states the Angel is “the uncreated one, the Angel of the covenant, the Son and Word of God.” Gray’s Concise Commentary says, “the angel of the Lord is none other than Jehovah Jesus.” Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary calls this “the second Person of the triune Godhead.” (Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-13/; Gill; Garner-Howes via StudyLight.org search result; Gray via StudyLight.org)

The Gospel Coalition presents a more nuanced Trinitarian theophany reading: the “messenger” (*mal’ak*) can designate function rather than ontological status. Context determines whether the messenger is a created angel or divine. Manoah’s conclusion “we have seen God” (v. 22), the refusal of a meal in favour of a sacrifice, and the name “wonderful” all point to divinity. TGC explains this as an Old Testament anticipation of the Trinity: “The Father speaks to them through the Son in the power of the Holy Spirit.” (TGC essay on Theophany, https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/theophany/ — from search excerpt)

## v. 4 — The Mother’s Obligations

The mother is told to abstain from wine, strong drink, and anything unclean — not for her own sake, but because **the child in the womb shares in what she consumes**. She is to participate in the Nazirite restrictions during pregnancy. Gill explains: “the child in the womb is nourished with the same the mother is; and as this child was to be a Nazarite from the womb, and even in it, his mother was to abstain.” Ellicott clarifies that “strong drink” (*shekar*, LXX *sikera*) means intoxicating liquor not made from grapes. (Gill; Ellicott, both cited above)

## v. 5 — A Nazirite from the Womb Who Will “Begin” Deliverance

The Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:1–21) normally involved three restrictions: no razor on the head, no wine or grape products, and no contact with the dead. Normally, the vow was voluntary and for a limited period. Samson’s case is unique: **the vow is imposed by God for life, from the womb**. (Enduring Word; Gill; Ellicott)

The phrase **“he will begin the deliverance of Israel”** is theologically significant. Morgan observed, “His ultimate failure was as certainly foreknown as was his opportunity.” Gill notes Samson’s salvation was “not complete and perfect; it was only begun by him, and carried on in the times of Eli, Samuel, and Saul, and perfected by David.” (Enduring Word; Gill)

Gill also draws a typological connection: Samson is a type of Christ — born of a barren woman (as Christ of a virgin), his birth foretold by an angel, consecrated from the womb; but Christ exceeds him by accomplishing a **complete** salvation. (Gill)

## vv. 6–7 — The Wife Reports to Manoah

She calls the visitor “a man of God” whose countenance was “like the angel of God, exceedingly awesome” — indicating she perceived him as human in form yet supernaturally majestic. She admits she did not ask his name or origin, perhaps from awe. Guzik notes: “the profound impact … was so much so that she did not ask questions.” (Enduring Word)

Her report adds one detail not recorded in the angel’s original words to her: **“from the womb until the day of his death”** — emphasising the lifelong nature of Samson’s Nazirite calling. Gill explains that the later cutting of his hair (Judges 16) did not contradict this because “these words are not a prophecy, but a precept; and besides, that affair happened but a little before his death.” (Gill; Enduring Word)

## vv. 8–10 — Manoah Prays; the Angel Returns

Manoah prays not out of unbelief but for **further instruction on how to raise the child**. He already believed the promise (“the child who is to be born”); he wanted practical direction. “He was desirous of knowing what was further to be done … which showed his readiness and cheerfulness to obey the will of God in all things.” (Gill)

God answers, but the Angel appears again **to the wife**, not to Manoah — alone in the field. Gill suggests this was so she would recognise him as the same visitor; had he appeared to Manoah alone, Manoah could not have identified him. The wife runs to fetch her husband. (Gill; Enduring Word)

The **Ligonier devotional** notes that Manoah’s reluctance to believe his wife’s initial report, and his later conclusion that they would die, “suggest that Manoah had a weak faith,” borne out later when he acquiesces to Samson’s desire for a Philistine wife (Judges 14:1–10). (Ligonier, https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/birth-of-samson — from search excerpt)

## vv. 11–12 — Manoah’s Question: “What Will Be the Boy’s Rule of Life and Mission?”

The literal Hebrew behind “rule of life” is *mishpat* (“judgment, ordering”). Manoah asks two things: what manner of life the boy should live, and what his work (mission) would be. Abarbinel (cited by Gill) says Manoah was asking to know future and wonderful things the child would do. (Gill; Ellicott)

## vv. 13–14 — The Angel’s Non-Answer

The Angel does **not** reveal Samson’s future mission. Instead, he repeats the instructions already given to the wife: she must abstain from vine products, wine, strong drink, and anything unclean. God honoured Manoah’s request for the Angel’s return but did not satisfy his curiosity about the future. Guzik comments: “He simply called Manoah and his wife to obey what God already told them to do.” (Enduring Word)

Verse 14 adds a detail not stated earlier: **“anything that comes from the vine”** — broader than wine alone, matching the full Nazirite prohibition in Numbers 6:3–4 (grapes, raisins, vinegar, kernels, husks). (Ellicott; Enduring Word)

## vv. 15–16 — Hospitality Refused; Sacrifice Directed

Manoah offers to prepare a young goat — either as a meal of hospitality or as a sacrifice (the Hebrew *‘asah* can mean either). The Angel refuses to eat but redirects: **“if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.”** Guzik sees this as evidence the Angel is God: He does not need a meal but accepts worship directed to the LORD. Ellicott notes that angels in Scripture “invariably discourage and reprove that ‘worship of angels’ (Colossians 2:18)” — citing Daniel 10, Revelation 19:10, and 22:8. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)

A narrative note explains: **“For Manoah did not know that it was the angel of the LORD.”** He still thought he was speaking to a human prophet.

## vv. 17–18 — “What Is Your Name?” / “It Is Wonderful”

Manoah asks the messenger’s name so that he might honour him later — likely with a gift, the common Eastern sense of “honour” (cf. Numbers 22:17). (Ellicott)

The Angel replies, **“Why do you ask my name, since it is beyond comprehension?”** The Hebrew word is *peli* (or *pil’i*), which means “wonderful, extraordinary, incomprehensible.” The KJV tradition renders it “secret”; the ASV/RSV/ESV/BSB tradition renders it “wonderful” or “beyond comprehension.” Ellicott notes this is the same word rendered “Wonderful” in Isaiah 9:6 — one of the Messianic titles. This is a key reason many conservative commentators see this as a Christophany. (Ellicott; Enduring Word; Gill)

Gill comments: “as his nature and essence as a divine Person, which may be meant by his name, is what passes knowledge, is infinite and incomprehensible.” (Gill)

## vv. 19–21 — The Sacrifice and the Angel’s Ascent

Manoah takes a young goat and grain offering and offers them **on a rock** to the LORD. Though Manoah was not a priest and this was not the Tabernacle, Gill says “all this was dispensed with … by the warrant of the angel” (cf. v. 16). Ellicott notes the rock (*tsur*) of v. 19 is now dignified as “the altar” (*mizbeach*) in v. 20. (Gill; Ellicott)

“The LORD did a marvelous thing” — likely a play on the word *peli* (“wonderful”) from v. 18. Gill (citing Kimchi and Josephus) says the wonder was fire coming from the rock to consume the sacrifice, as with Gideon in Judges 6:21. (Gill; Ellicott)

**The Angel ascends in the flame.** This is the climactic revelation: the messenger who would not eat human food now ascends in the sacrificial flame heavenward — a visible demonstration that the offering was accepted and that the messenger was divine. Manoah and his wife fall on their faces. Only now does Manoah realise the visitor was the Angel of the LORD. (Enduring Word; Gill; Ellicott)

Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word) draws two pastoral applications from this passage: (1) “Oftentimes we pray for blessings which will make us tremble when we receive them”; (2) “Very frequently deep prostration of spirit is the forerunner of some remarkable blessing.” (Enduring Word; Spurgeon’s full sermon excerpt is at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/judges-13.html)

## vv. 22–23 — Manoah’s Terror and His Wife’s Wise Response

**v. 22:** Manoah cries, “We are going to die, for we have seen God!” — reflecting the belief drawn from Exodus 33:20 (“no man shall see Me and live”). His fear is traditional and sincere. (Enduring Word; Ellicott; Gill)

**v. 23:** His wife’s reply is remarkably logical and faith-filled. She offers **three arguments** (Spurgeon calls them “three strings to her bow”):

1. **Accepted sacrifices:** “If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and grain offering from our hands.”
2. **Gracious revelations:** “Nor would He have shown us all these things.”
3. **Precious promises:** “Nor would He have spoken to us this way.”

Guzik comments: “She understood that God had not done so much for them to abandon them now. God’s past work in our lives is a promise of His future care and blessing for us.” (Enduring Word)

Spurgeon preached an entire sermon on these verses titled “Her Excellent Argument,” praising Manoah’s wife as the stronger believer of the two: “She was the weaker vessel by nature, but she was the stronger believer, and probably that was why the angel was sent to her.” He notes, “great faith is in many instances subject to fits” — even Manoah, who had “strong faith,” momentarily collapsed in terror. Spurgeon also draws the gospel parallel: “If the LORD wanted to do you evil, He would have never accepted an offering on your behalf – the offering of Jesus on the cross.” (Spurgeon, via Enduring Word and StudyLight.org search excerpt)

The Ligonier devotional notes that Manoah “jumped to the wrong conclusion … though his wife corrected him,” consistent with their assessment of his weak faith. (Ligonier, https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/birth-of-samson)

## v. 24 — Samson’s Birth and Early Years

The woman names him Samson (Hebrew *Shimshon*). Ellicott notes various etymologies: Josephus derives it from a root meaning “strong”; Jerome derived it from *shemesh* (“sun”) + *on* (“strength”) = “strength of the sun”; the more probable meaning is “sunny” or “little sun.” The Rabbis said he was “named after the name of God, who is called sun and shield of Israel” (Psalm 84:12). The mother names the child — as with other significant births (Genesis 29:32–35; Luke 1:60). (Ellicott)

“The LORD blessed him” — Ellicott clarifies these are blessings of health, strength, and courage, not necessarily spiritual maturity. Samson does not match Samuel or John the Baptist in character development. (Ellicott)

## v. 25 — The Spirit of the LORD Begins to Stir Him

The Hebrew verb *pa’am* means “to agitate, impel, thrust” — used elsewhere of troubling dreams (Genesis 41:8; Daniel 2:1). The Targum of Jonathan paraphrases, “The spirit of courage from Jehovah.” Ellicott notes the word “implies vehement and overwhelming impulses to noble deeds” which came upon Samson “at times” (as seen later in 14:6; 15:14; 16:20). Luther rendered it “fing an ihn zu treiben” — “began to drive him.” (Ellicott)

**Mahaneh-dan** (“Camp of Dan”) is the location between Zorah and Eshtaol. Ellicott explains this place-name likely originated from the migration of the hard-pressed Danites (see Judges 18:11–12), which occurred before Samson’s time. Samson would have grown up among the remnant of Dan that remained in their original territory. (Ellicott)

Guzik emphasises: “Samson is often imagined as a man with huge, rippling muscles; but others couldn’t understand why he was so strong. It is reasonable to think that he did not look very strong. Whether he looked strong or not, it was the Spirit of God who made him strong.” (Enduring Word)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**The Angel of the LORD: Christ or Created Angel?** The dominant view among the sources reviewed — Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word), Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes, Gray’s), and Reformed (TGC) — is that this was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. TGC articulates this in explicitly Trinitarian terms, seeing the Angel as God the Son sent by God the Father. The alternative view (that this was a created angelic messenger with divine authority) is held by some, though no source consulted here explicitly argues it for Judges 13. The Ligonier devotional treats the passage as a genuine angelic visit without explicitly calling it a Christophany.

**Manoah’s Faith — Weak or Strong?** The Ligonier Reformed reading sees Manoah as having “weak faith” (reluctance to believe his wife, wrong conclusion about dying, later failure with Samson’s marriage). Spurgeon, by contrast, calls Manoah “strong in faith” who had a momentary “fit” of fear — “great faith is in many instances subject to fits.” Both agree, however, that Manoah’s wife is the theological hero of the passage. (Ligonier; Spurgeon via Enduring Word)

**“Secret” vs. “Wonderful” (v. 18):** The KJV tradition (“secret”) follows the idea of a hidden, unknowable name. Modern translations (“wonderful” / “beyond comprehension”) follow the reading that connects this to the Messianic title in Isaiah 9:6. All the commentaries reviewed lean toward “wonderful.”
